title: Chinese Cinderella
author: Adeline Yen Mah
blurb: A neglected daughter finally wins her father’s approval through success at school in 1950s Hong Kong.
source: A neglected daughter wins her father's approval through academic success
heading: From Chinese Cinderella - Adeline Yen Mah
context: Growing up in a wealthy family in 1950s Hong Kong, Mah should have had an enviable childhood, but she was rejected by her dominating stepmother and despised by her brothers and sisters. She was sent to a boarding school and left there. In this extract from her autobiography she relates one of the few occasions when she went home.

paragraphs.html: Time went by relentlessly and it was Saturday again. Eight weeks more and it would be the end of term ... in my case perhaps the end of school forever.

Four of us were playing Monopoly. My heart was not in it and I was losing steadily. Outside it was hot and there was a warm wind blowing. The radio warned of a possible typhoon the next day. It was my turn and I threw the dice. As I played, the thought of leaving school throbbed at the back of my mind like a persistent toothache.
'Adeline!' Ma-mien Valentino was calling.
'You can't go now,' Mary protested. 'For once I'm winning. One, two, three, four. Good! You've landed on my property. Thirty-five dollars, please. Oh, good afternoon, Mother Valentino!'
We all stood up and greeted her.
'Adeline, didn't you hear me call you? Hurry up downstairs! Your chauffeur is waiting to take you home!'
Full of foreboding, I ran downstairs as in a nightmare, wondering who had died this time. Father's chauffeur assured me everyone was healthy.
'Then why are you taking me home?' I asked.
'How should I know?' he answered defensively, shrugging his shoulders. 'Your guess is as good as mine. They give the orders and I carry them out.'
During the short drive home, my heart was full of dread and I wondered what I had done wrong. Our car stopped at an elegant villa at mid-level, halfway up the hill between the peak and the harbour.
'Where are we?' I asked foolishly.
'Don't you know anything?' the chauffeur replied rudely. 'This is your new home. Your parents moved here a few months ago.'
'I had forgotten,' I said as I got out.
Ah Gum opened the door. Inside, it was quiet and cool.
'Where is everyone?'
'Your mother is out playing bridge. Your two brothers and Little Sister are sunbathing by the swimming-pool. Your father is in his room and wants to see you as soon as you get home.'
'See me in his room?' I was overwhelmed by the thought that I had been summoned by Father to enter the Holy of Holies — a place to which I had never been invited. Why? ...

Timidly, I knocked on the door. Father was alone, looking relaxed in his slippers and bathrobe, reading a newspaper. He smiled as I entered and I saw he was in a happy mood. I breathed a small sigh of relief at first but became uneasy again when I wondered why he was being so nice, thinking, Is this a giant ruse on his part to trick me? Dare I let my guard down?
'Sit down! Sit down!' He pointed to a chair. 'Don't look so scared. Here, take a look at this! They're writing about someone we both know, I think.'
He handed me the day's newspaper and there, in one corner, I saw my name ADELINE YEN in capital letters prominently displayed.

'It was announced today that 14-year-old Hong Kong schoolgirl ADELINE JUN-LING YEN of Sacred Heart Canossian School, Caine Road, Hong Kong, has won first prize in the International Play-writing Competition held in London, England, for the 1951—1952 school year. It is the first time that any local Chinese student from Hong Kong has won such a prestigious event. Besides a medal, the prize comes with a cash reward of FIFTY ENGLISH POUNDS. Our sincere congratulations, ADELINE YEN, for bringing honour to Hong Kong. We are proud of you'.
Is it possible? Am I dreaming? Me, the winner?

'I was going up the lift this morning with my friend C.Y. Tung when he showed me this article and asked me, "Is the winner Adeline Jun-ling Yen related to you? The two of you have the same uncommon last name." Now C.Y. himself has a few children about your age but so far none of them has won an international literary prize, as far as I know. So I was quite pleased to tell him you are my daughter. Well done!'

He looked radiant. For once, he was proud of me. In front of his revered colleague, C.Y. Tung, a prominent fellow businessman also from Shanghai, I had given him face. I thought, Is this the big moment I have been waiting for? My whole being vibrated with all the joy in the world. I only had to stretch out my hand to reach the stars.
'Tell me, how did you do it?' he continued. 'How come you won?'

'Well, the rules and regulations were so very complicated. One really has to be dedicated just to understand what they want. Perhaps I was the only one determined enough to enter and there were no other competitors!'
He laughed approvingly. 'I doubt it very much but that's a good answer.'
'Please, Father,' I asked boldly, thinking it was now or never. 'May I go to university in England too, just like my brothers?'
'I do believe you have potential. Tell me, what would you study?'

My heart gave a giant lurch as it dawned on me that he was agreeing to let me go. How marvellous it was simply to be alive! Study? I thought. Going to England is like entering heaven. Does it matter what you do after you get to heaven?
But Father was expecting an answer. What about creative writing? After all, I had just won first prize in an international writing competition!
'I plan to study literature. I'll be a writer.'

'Writer!' he scoffed. 'You are going to starve! What language are you going to write in and who is going to read your writing? Though you may think you're an expert in both Chinese and English, your Chinese is actually rather elementary. As for your English, don't you think the native English speakers can write better than you?'
I waited in silence. I did not wish to contradict him.

'You will go to England with Third Brother this summer and you will go to medical school. After you graduate, you will specialise in obstetrics. Women will always be having babies. Women patients prefer women doctors. You will learn to deliver their babies. That's a foolproof profession for you. Don't you agree?'

Agree? Of course I agreed. Apparently, he had it all planned out. As long as he let me go to university in England, I would study anything he wished. How did that line go in Wordsworth's poem? Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive.
'Father, I shall go to medical school in England and become a doctor. Thank you very, very much.'

relentlessly.what: 'Relentlessly' (without pause or mercy) makes time sound like a force chasing her.
relentlessly.effect: We feel the weeks running out before we even know why.

perhaps-forever.quote: perhaps the end of school forever
perhaps-forever.what: The ellipsis (...) makes her pause before the worst thought: losing school 'forever'.
perhaps-forever.effect: 'Perhaps' shows her future is out of her hands, and school is her lifeline.

heart-not.quote: My heart was not in it
heart-not.what: She is with friends, yet her thoughts are somewhere else.
heart-not.effect: Worry spoils even an ordinary Saturday game, so we sense her fear never leaves her.

throbbed-toothache.quote: throbbed at the back of my mind like a persistent toothache
throbbed-toothache.what: 'Throbbed' gives her worry a beat, like pain that pulses and will not stop.
throbbed-toothache.effect: Everyone knows a toothache cannot be ignored, so we feel her worry as constant.

chauffeur-waiting.quote: Your chauffeur is waiting to take you home!
chauffeur-waiting.what: Being fetched home without warning breaks up the game and starts the main action.
chauffeur-waiting.effect: Most children would be pleased, so her alarm tells us home means danger.

full-foreboding.what: 'Foreboding' (a feeling that something bad will happen) comes before anyone tells her anything.
full-foreboding.effect: Her fear is automatic, as if a call home has always meant trouble.

as-nightmare.what: The simile suggests moving helplessly towards something terrible, as in a bad dream.
as-nightmare.effect: We feel her panic, as if the moment is too frightening to be real.

who-died.what: 'This time' hints that she has been called home with news of a death before.
who-died.effect: Her calm guess is shocking: she expects nothing good from home.

your-guess.quote: Your guess is as good as mine. They give the orders and I carry them out
your-guess.what: 'They give the orders' shows a household run by commands from the top.
your-guess.effect: Nobody tells Adeline anything, so she is as powerless as the servants.

heart-dread.quote: my heart was full of dread
heart-dread.what: Fear fills her heart, and she assumes she has done something wrong.
heart-dread.effect: She blames herself before knowing the facts, like a child trained to expect punishment.

foolishly.what: She calls herself foolish for not knowing where her own family lives.
foolishly.effect: Her parents failed to tell her, yet she takes the blame.

dont-know-anything.what: The chauffeur mocks her with a scornful question, and Mah stresses he spoke 'rudely'.
dont-know-anything.effect: Even servants copy the family's contempt, so her low status is clear to all.

i-forgotten.what: She takes the blame for not knowing about a house move months ago.
i-forgotten.effect: We see what she covers up: nobody told her or brought her home.

father-room.quote: Your father is in his room and wants to see you as soon as you get home
father-room.what: Ah Gum saves Father for last, and his wish to see her 'as soon as' is urgent.
father-room.effect: Like Adeline, we expect punishment and wait to learn what she has done.

holy-holies.what: The Holy of Holies was the Temple's inner room, which only the high priest could enter.
holy-holies.effect: Father seems god-like and out of reach, so the invitation is both honour and terror.

happy-mood.what: After all the build-up of fear, Father is relaxed and smiling.
happy-mood.effect: His good mood is so rare that it feels almost threatening.

small-sigh.what: 'Small' limits her relief, and the worry returns straight away.
small-sigh.effect: She cannot trust a good moment with her father.

giant-ruse.quote: Is this a giant ruse on his part to trick me? Dare I let my guard down?
giant-ruse.what: A 'ruse' is a trick, and 'Dare' makes relaxing sound risky.
giant-ruse.effect: It is sad that her own father's smile feels like a trap.

dont-scared.what: Father gives her a command (an imperative) because her fear shows on her face.
dont-scared.effect: Even his kindness is an order, and he seems unaware he caused her fear.

adeline-capitals.quote: ADELINE YEN in capital letters prominently displayed
adeline-capitals.what: Mah copies the newspaper's capitals, so her name jumps out at us too.
adeline-capitals.effect: A girl ignored at home is suddenly picked out in public.

prestigious-event.what: Formal words like 'prestigious' (highly respected) mark this as a public honour.
prestigious-event.effect: This is the kind of success Father's world values, which explains his change.

fifty-pounds.what: The prize money is in capitals, just like her name.
fifty-pounds.effect: Father is a businessman, so the money may matter to him as much as the honour.

bringing-honour.what: The newspaper says one girl's success honours the whole community.
bringing-honour.effect: If she honours Hong Kong, she also honours her family, which is what Father wants.

is-possible.quote: Is it possible? Am I dreaming? Me, the winner?
is-possible.what: Three quick questions shrink to 'Me, the winner?', as if she cannot finish the thought.
is-possible.effect: Someone treated as worthless cannot believe she has won.

well-done.what: Father's two words of praise come after a long story about his own pride.
well-done.effect: They mean everything to her, yet they come because she made him look good.

radiant.what: 'Radiant' means glowing, a huge change from the cold father we expected.
radiant.effect: His pleasure lights her up too, showing how his mood controls hers.

for-once.quote: For once, he was proud of me
for-once.what: This short sentence is the turning point, and 'For once' says it never happened before.
for-once.effect: Two small words sum up a lifetime of rejection.

given-face.what: 'Face' means respect and reputation in Chinese culture, and her prize raises Father's.
given-face.effect: We may feel uneasy that his pride is partly about himself.

whole-being.quote: My whole being vibrated with all the joy in the world
whole-being.what: 'All the joy in the world' is hyperbole (deliberate exaggeration), and 'vibrated' makes joy physical.
whole-being.effect: After so much fear, the happiness overwhelms her.

stretch-stars.quote: I only had to stretch out my hand to reach the stars
stretch-stars.what: The stars stand for her biggest hopes, suddenly within easy reach.
stretch-stars.effect: We share her hope, but sense that hopes raised this high can fall far.

only-one.quote: Perhaps I was the only one determined enough to enter and there were no other competitors!
only-one.what: Self-deprecation (making fun of yourself) lets her play down the win without seeming boastful.
only-one.effect: It shows a clever girl who has learned that modesty is safe with Father.

doubt-it.quote: I doubt it very much but that's a good answer
doubt-it.what: Father laughs and seems to like her modesty as much as her prize.
doubt-it.effect: She earns his warmth by being humble and pleasing him.

now-never.what: The idiom shows her seizing his rare good mood as her one chance.
now-never.effect: Everything she wants now hangs on a single question.

may-i-go.quote: May I go to university in England too, just like my brothers?
may-i-go.what: 'Too' and 'just like my brothers' show the boys' places are already settled.
may-i-go.effect: The boys go without asking while she must plead, exposing the family's unfairness.

have-potential.quote: I do believe you have potential
have-potential.what: 'Potential' praises what she might become, then he moves straight on.
have-potential.effect: Even his warmest words hold something back.

heart-lurch.quote: My heart gave a giant lurch
heart-lurch.what: A 'lurch' is a sudden, jerky movement, and 'giant' stresses its force.
heart-lurch.effect: Her body reacts before her mind catches up with the news.

how-marvellous.quote: How marvellous it was simply to be alive!
how-marvellous.what: Earlier the same afternoon she ran downstairs wondering who had died.
how-marvellous.effect: The swing from dread to joy hints at how low she felt before.

entering-heaven.quote: Going to England is like entering heaven. Does it matter what you do after you get to heaven?
entering-heaven.what: Her question suggests the subject hardly matters once she reaches England.
entering-heaven.effect: If leaving home feels like heaven, her life there must be miserable.

writer-scoffed.quote: Writer!' he scoffed. 'You are going to starve!
writer-scoffed.what: 'Scoffed' means mocked, and the threat that she will 'starve' treats her dream as foolish.
writer-scoffed.effect: He dismisses the very talent that won the prize he is so proud of.

rather-elementary.quote: your Chinese is actually rather elementary
rather-elementary.what: Father calls her Chinese basic, then doubts her English as well.
rather-elementary.effect: He leaves her no language to write in, clearing the way for his plan.

waited-silence.quote: I waited in silence. I did not wish to contradict him
waited-silence.what: Two short, flat sentences follow Father's long speech.
waited-silence.effect: Her silence shows she has learned that arguing with Father is never safe.

medical-school.quote: you will go to medical school
medical-school.what: Father repeats 'you will', turning each step of her future into an order.
medical-school.effect: Her prize wins her England, while her career is chosen for her.

foolproof-profession.quote: That's a foolproof profession for you. Don't you agree?
foolproof-profession.what: 'Don't you agree?' sounds like a question, yet only one answer is allowed.
foolproof-profession.effect: He pretends to ask her opinion after deciding everything.

agree-course.what: She echoes his word and answers at once, perhaps with a trace of irony.
agree-course.effect: Refusing could cost her England, so agreeing is the only safe answer.

apparently-planned.quote: Apparently, he had it all planned out
apparently-planned.what: 'Apparently' shows her slowly realising that Father had already decided.
apparently-planned.effect: She is free to leave, yet he still controls her from a distance.

bliss-dawn.quote: Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive
bliss-dawn.what: She quotes Wordsworth's line about the hope of the French Revolution.
bliss-dawn.effect: Just after Father mocked her writing, it proves she has the literary mind he dismissed.

father-shall.quote: Father, I shall go to medical school in England and become a doctor. Thank you very, very much
father-shall.what: Her final words are formal and repeat his plan back to him.
father-shall.effect: The doubled 'very' is grateful and sad: she thanks him for a future he chose.

obstetrics.meaning: The branch of medicine that cares for women in pregnancy and childbirth.
obstetrics.note: Father picks this exact specialism for her before she has even started medical school.
obstetrics.effect: His reason is that 'Women will always be having babies', so even in medicine he limits her.

overview.heading: Why Mah wrote this
overview.intro: Mah shows what it was like to be an unwanted daughter.

points.label: To show neglect
points.text: "I had forgotten" shows how completely she was left out of family life.

points.label: To explain Chinese values
points.text: "I had given him face" shows that her worth to Father is tied to his reputation.

points.label: To show limits on girls
points.text: "That's a foolproof profession for you" shows Father choosing a career he thinks suits a girl.

overview.heading: Who she is writing for
overview.intro: Mah writes for several kinds of reader.

points.label: Readers new to Chinese culture
points.text: "I had given him face" and the Hong Kong setting open a window on a different culture.

points.label: Anyone wanting a parent's approval
points.text: "For once, he was proud of me" captures a longing almost every reader recognises.

points.label: Young women facing limits
points.text: "May I go to university in England too" speaks to girls who have had to fight for equal chances.

overview.heading: How her tone changes
overview.intro: Her voice moves from fear, to joy, to quiet acceptance.

points.label: Fearful child
points.text: "Full of foreboding" shows a girl who expects punishment whenever she is called home.

points.label: Disbelieving winner
points.text: "Is it possible? Am I dreaming?" shows she cannot believe good news about herself.

points.label: Joyful daughter
points.text: "My heart gave a giant lurch" shows joy so strong she feels it in her body.

points.label: Obedient survivor
points.text: "Of course I agreed" shows her accepting Father's plan so she can still escape.

overview.heading: Language choices
overview.intro: Mah uses images that let us feel her emotions.

points.label: Feelings made physical
points.text: "like a persistent toothache" turns her worry into a pain we all know.

points.label: Religious imagery
points.text: "Holy of Holies" and "entering heaven" make Father seem god-like and England seem like paradise.

points.label: Reaching for the stars
points.text: "stretch out my hand to reach the stars" shows her dreams suddenly within reach.

points.label: Literary allusion
points.text: "Bliss was it in that dawn" borrows Wordsworth's words and proves her love of literature.

overview.heading: How it is organised
overview.intro: The extract swings from dread to triumph, then to compromise.

points.label: Fear to triumph
points.text: "Your chauffeur is waiting" starts a tension that the prize news suddenly releases.

points.label: Turning point
points.text: "For once, he was proud of me" marks the moment everything changes between them.

points.label: Dream refused, plan imposed
points.text: "you will go to medical school" replaces her writing dream with Father's plan.

points.label: Grateful ending
points.text: "Thank you very, very much" ends the extract with her accepting the compromise.
